analysis.one_liner: Gives public-company shareholders annual votes on executive pay, golden parachutes, and board nominations.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee — no hearing, no vote — and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: Written in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, this bill would have required public companies to let shareholders vote every year on executive pay packages, vote separately on executive 'golden parachute' payouts during mergers, and made it easier for large shareholders to nominate people for the board of directors. It would also have forced listed companies to meet new governance standards: an independent board chair, directors elected every year, directors who lose a majority vote leaving the board, and a risk committee made up entirely of independent directors. The Senate Banking Committee never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders of public companies — which the bill itself notes includes millions of Americans who own stock through 401(k) plans, pension funds, and direct investments. They would get an annual, though non-binding, vote on executive compensation, a vote on merger-related executive payouts, and a route for large shareholders to place nominees on company proxy ballots. The governance standards would also give investors a board more answerable to them.

how_it_helps.text: Every public company would have to put executive compensation up for a separate shareholder vote at least annually, giving owners a visible say on pay packages.
In mergers and asset sales, any special executive compensation deals would have to be disclosed in plain form and put to a separate shareholder vote.

The SEC would have to write rules letting shareholders who own at least 1% of a company for two years use the company's own proxy materials to nominate board candidates, instead of paying for their own mailings.

Companies would lose their stock listings unless they had an independent board chair who had never been a company executive, directors up for election every year, majority-vote elections with losing directors resigning, and a fully independent risk committee overseeing risk management.

analysis.who_pays: Corporate executives and boards of directors, who would lose unilateral control over pay packages, merger payouts, and board composition, and would face annual accountability votes. Public companies would also bear the cost of new governance and compliance practices, though the SEC could exempt smaller issuers.

drawbacks.text: The votes on executive pay and golden parachutes are explicitly non-binding: the board cannot be forced to change anything no matter how shareholders vote.

The proxy access right is limited to shareholders holding at least 1% of the company for two years, which in practice favors large institutional investors and does little for an individual retirement saver holding a few shares.

The listing standards would impose real compliance costs on public companies, and honest supporters of tighter governance after a crisis would acknowledge some of those costs fall on ordinary shareholders as owners of the companies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The shareholder tools created here are modest by design — the pay votes cannot bind a board, and proxy access is limited to large holders — so the direct benefits to ordinary retirement savers are real but limited, mainly pressure and sunlight rather than control. The governance standards (annual elections, majority vote, independent risk committee) are the strongest part. The costs are compliance burdens for companies, which shareholders ultimately share. On balance the scales tip toward shareholders, with legitimate questions about whether the added process is worth the cost for smaller firms.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in May 2009 and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Charles Schumer introduced the bill on May 19, 2009, for himself and Sen. Maria Cantwell.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
That was the bill's last action of any kind: it received no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action through the end of the 111th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives and boards of public companies are better off, because they kept sole control over executive pay, merger payouts, and board elections without ever facing the shareholder votes or governance standards the bill would have imposed.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
against.role: Chairman, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing or markup on it; the referral was the bill's final action.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators sponsored the bill and no other senators are recorded as supporting or opposing it; no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of the fight never appeared in the record.

industries.industry: Public company executives and boards of directors
industries.note: The bill would strip executives and boards of unilateral power over their own pay, merger payouts, and board elections, subjecting all of it to shareholder votes and new independence rules. Their interest ran against the bill, and with the bill dead they kept full control.

industries.industry: Large institutional investors (pension funds, mutual funds, asset managers)
industries.note: The proxy access provision would give shareholders holding 1% for two years a company-funded route to nominate directors — a power only large institutions could realistically use. Ordinary retirement savers would benefit mainly through those institutions acting on their behalf.
